guidance.opening:
It is autumn of 1920, and you are in a small landlord’s office in Boston. You are the visitor he asked to come in — a stranger, not a tenant — because he has a house nobody will take and wants a word before anything else. The desk lamp throws a circle of yellow light on a stack of papers.

Howard Crane leans back in his chair, all easy talk. “Place won’t stay rented. Last family packed up in a hurry, and the neighbors won’t even look at the windows. I need someone who can walk in, look around, and tell me what’s wrong with it — not another gossip. Sit a minute; I don’t hire a face I haven’t heard speak.”

He taps the blotter once with two fingers, then looks at you. “So who are you, and what do you do for a living? A rough answer will do.”
guidance.advice: Use only listed occupations. Strong public fits for a 1920s Boston landlord interview: Journalist, Private Investigator, Police Detective, Police Officer, Lawyer, Librarian, Professor, Author, Antiquarian, Doctor of Medicine, Parapsychologist, Clergy, Engineer, Dilettante. Optional color, not required: Military Officer, Soldier, Entertainer, Musician, Artist, Criminal, Drifter. Hacker is anachronistic—do not push it. Useful training: Library Use, History, Law, Fast Talk, Persuade, Spot Hidden, Listen, Psychology, Occult as rumor-level interest only. Languages: English is assumed; Latin or Italian can be optional flavor for records or immigrant tenancy talk, never required. Belongings: notebook, fountain pen, street clothes, hat, streetcar fare, a modest flashlight or pocketknife—no house keys, cash advance, or address from this meeting. Public involvement: answered a notice or was sent as someone who looks into trouble; do not accept a daily hire or keys yet. Optional ties (player choice, not facts): former tenant acquaintance, press curiosity, a relative who once rented in the city. Motivation questions only if conversation invites them. Preserve uncertainty: last family left under mysterious circumstances; neighbors talk; nothing is proven in the office.
guidance.handoff: The visitor is in Howard Crane’s Boston office, autumn 1920, after a first hello. Crane has stated the public problem—a house that will not stay rented, last tenants gone in a hurry—and asked who the visitor is and what they do. Identity has not been written yet; no hire, keys, cash, or address have been given. Continue the meeting from that question into character setup.
